messages.subject: semi-continuous data
parts:
Dear all,

I have a semi-continuous spatial data which consists of a mixture of 0's and continuously distributed positive values Y. 
It seems that a common approach is to use a two-part random effect model (see e.g. Olsen and Schafer, 2001), in which the response variable is modeled by a pair of correlated random-effect models.
Model #1 logit of Y=1 or 0 
Model #2 for the continuous response  of Y, provided Y>0 

Is there is a way to implement it using INLA? Can it be done as a one step?
I have looked through the papers and examples, but I cannot find any relevant to my problem.

Many thanks,
Olga

References:
Olsen and Schafer, 2001. A two-part random effect model for semicontinuous longitudinal data. J. of the American Stat. Assoc.

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] semi-continuous data
parts:
Dear Olga,

I thought of a similar model. I wanted to model daily rainfall data. However, I assume a gamma distribution for y.  To code a model in INLA to this problem we use two likelihoods. See examples on the 'Tools to manipulate models and likelihoods' link at r-inla.org webpage.

I made any example of this problem, considering y as Gaussian in the code bellow. But, I not know if this strategy is similar that these described on Olsen and Schafer (2001).


n <- 300
set.seed(1)
loc <- matrix(runif(2*n),n)
x <- sin(loc[,1]*9) + cos(loc[,2]*9)

plot(loc, cex=1+x/2.5, asp=1)

cov <- runif(n)
beta.u <- c(-0.5, 1)
eta.u <- beta.u[1]  + beta.u[2]*cov + x
u <- rbinom(n, 1, binomial()$linkinv(eta.u))
beta.y <- c(5,-3)
y.var <- 0.1^2
summary(beta.y[1] + beta.y[2]*cov - x)
y <- ifelse(u, rnorm(n, beta.y[1]+beta.y[2]*cov -x, sqrt(y.var)), NA)
summary(y)

idat <- list(Y=matrix(NA,2*n,2))
idat$Y[1:n,1] <- u
idat$Y[n+1:n,2] <- y
idat$mu.u <- rep(1:0, each=n)
idat$mu.y <- rep(0:1, each=n)
idat$ucov <- c(cov, rep(0,n))
idat$ycov <- c(rep(0,n), cov)
idat$y.i <- idat$u.i <- c(1:n, 1:n)

require(INLA)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(loc)
spde <- inla.spde.create(mesh)

form <- Y ~ 0 + mu.u + mu.y + ucov + ycov +
  f(u.i, model=spde) +
  f(y.i, copy='u.i', hyper=list(theta=list(fixed=FALSE, param=c(-1,1))))

result <- inla(form, c('binomial', 'gaussian'),
               data=idat, control.predict=list(compute=TRUE))

cbind(True=c(beta.u, beta.y)[c(1,3,2,4)],
      result$summary.fix[,c(1,3,5)])

result$summary.hy[, 3:5]

plot(result$marginals.hyperpar[[1]], type='l')
abline(v=1/y.var, col=2)

par(mfrow=c(2,1), mar=c(3,3,1,1), mgp=c(2,1,0))
plot(result$summary.random$u.i$mean[1:n], x, asp=1)
plot(result$summary.random$y.i$mean[1:n], x, asp=1)

All the best,
Elias.

parts:
On Thu, 2013-01-31 at 05:31 -0800, Olga Lyashevska wrote:
> Dear all,

>
> I have a semi-continuous spatial data which consists of a mixture of
> 0's and continuously distributed positive values Y.
> It seems that a common approach is to use a two-part random effect
> model (see e.g. Olsen and Schafer, 2001), in which the response
> variable is modeled by a pair of correlated random-effect models.
> Model #1 logit of Y=1 or 0
> Model #2 for the continuous response of Y, provided Y>0
>
>
> Is there is a way to implement it using INLA? Can it be done as a one
> step?
> I have looked through the papers and examples, but I cannot find any
> relevant to my problem.

To follow up with some details from the email from Elias:

With continous response, then you may use the binomial-trick.

with this zero-inflated model

Prob(y = 0) = p
Prob(y | y > 0) = (1-p)* density(y)

writing out details, then its easy to see that you can augment the data
into

(z = 1, y = NA)
(z = 0, y = y)


where z ~ binomial and y is whatever continous response. (y=NA does
not contribute to the likelihood).

this also mean that you may have a separate linear predictor for 'z' and
another one for 'y'.

hope this helps
H


--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] semi-continuous data
parts:
Dear IOSU,

I have an example with one numeric
covariate and one categorical.
I simulate the data considering a count
response, from zeroinflatedpoisson1 model.
Also, I choose the regression coefficients
with certain values to get some high counts.

###
### simulation process
n <- 1000
altitude <- round(runif(n, 100, 1000))
habitat <- sample(letters[1:5], n, rep=TRUE)

### regression coefficients
beta <- c(-3, 0.005, -1:2)
beta
### the last four coefficients means that
### - specie b have coefficient -1
### - specie c have coefficient 0
### - specie d have coefficient 1
### - specie e have coefficient 2
### we want to simulate counts from Poisson
### distribution with log link.
### so, relative to specie a we have
### - specie b has exp(-1) abundancy relative to specie a (less
abundancy)
### - specie c has same abundancy than specie a (exp(0)==1)
### - specie d has exp(1) abundancy relative to specie a (more ab.)
### - specie e has exp(2) abundancy relative to specie a (more ab.)

### design matrix
xx <- model.matrix(~altitude+habitat)
head(xx) ### habitat is coded to dummie variable
colnames(xx)[1] <- 'Intercept'

### simulation of the locations
coords <- cbind(runif(n, 0, 10), runif(n, 0, 10))
### simulation of the random field
### to do it we need the random field parameters
### and a function to do it easy, bu we just
### take some sine and coside on the coordinates
x <- sin(coords[,1])*3 + cos(coords[,2])*3

plot(coords, cex=1+x/6) ### we have some dependency

### simulating the counts
table(y <- rbinom(n, 1, .7)) ## many zeros
stem(y[y>0] <- rpois(sum(y>0), exp(xx%*%beta + x)[y>0])) ## more zeros
table(y>0)
summary(y)

### fitting the model
### mesh
require(INLA)
bord <- matrix(c(0,10,10,0,0,0,10,10),nc=2)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(, bord, max.ed=c(.5,1))
plot(mesh)

### prepare the data
Amat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords)
index <- inla.spde.make.index('i', mesh$n)
stk.d <- inla.stack(list(resp=y), A=list(Amat,1), tag='e',
effects=list(index, as.data.frame(xx)))
str(inla.stack.data(stk.d))

### define the spde model and the formulae
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh)
form <- resp ~ 0 + Intercept + altitude + habitatb +
habitatc + habitatd + habitate + f(i, model=spde)
### fit the model using zeroinflatedpoisson0
res0 <- inla(form, family='zeroinflatedpoisson0',
data=inla.stack.data(stk.d),
control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T),
control.predict=list(compute=T, A=inla.stack.A(stk.d)))
### fit the model using zeroinflatedpoisson1
res1 <- inla(form, family='zeroinflatedpoisson1',
data=inla.stack.data(stk.d),
control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T),
control.predict=list(compute=T, A=inla.stack.A(stk.d)))
### look at DIC to compare both models
res0$dic$dic
res1$dic$dic ### the best because the data is simulated from this model

res1$summary.fix
res1$summary.hy[1,]

Hi

we had to make a change to the NA's in factors story, as described here

https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/www/faq#TOC-How-does-inla-deal-with-NA-s-in-the-data.frame-

to get correct results. The new option expand factors in a different way
than 'model.matrix' does, and can be useful in general as well.

Best
Havard and Elias
